passage:
Varun,
I'm writing because you went all serious on me after tuition and I didn't like it. So here's the truth. Yes, I vape sometimes. It was only at Karma's parties at first. Then maybe Fridays. And okay, lately a few times after tuition too.
But it's not a problem. I can stop whenever I want. I stopped for the whole Losar holiday, didn't I?
Honestly, compared to Tashi and that lot, I barely do anything. They do it in the school toilets. I would never.
It just helps me switch off after mock exams. Everyone needs something.
So you don't need to look at me like that, or tell Amala. I've got it under control.
Your friend (still),
Pema
PS. Can you lend me 300 till next week? I'll explain later.

qa.q: Where did Pema vape at first?
qa.a: Only at Karma's parties at first.

qa.q: Why does Pema keep comparing to Tashi and the others?
qa.a: Comparing makes Pema's own use seem small, which helps Pema avoid looking at how often it has started happening.

qa.q: What could Varun do after reading this letter?
qa.a: Varun could stay a calm, caring friend, gently point out how 'only parties' became several times a week, and encourage Pema to talk to Amala or a school counsellor.

qa.q: How might Varun feel reading the letter, especially the PS?
qa.a: Varun may feel pushed away and worried, since the letter insists everything is under control while the PS asking for money hints that it is growing.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose vaping has grown from parties to several times a week, minimising it and comparing with friends who do it more.

passage:
Pooja, relax, it's not like that. This is Irfan you're talking to, not some villain from a film. It's just beer with the cricket lot on Saturdays after nets. Everyone does it.
Okay, and sometimes Wednesdays now, because Wednesdays are the worst, with Physics tuition and Abba checking my marks. But I can stop whenever I want. Last month I didn't touch anything for a whole week when Ammi was unwell. Did anything happen? No.
You should see Faisal. He drinks before school sometimes. Before school, Pooja. That's a problem. Me, I just like to switch off.
You're making a face. Why are you making that face?
...Fine. It was three times last week, not two. But that was because of the unit test. That week doesn't count.
Just don't tell Ammi, okay? She's already stressed about everything.

qa.q: How many times did Irfan admit to drinking last week?
qa.a: Three times last week, not two.

qa.q: Why does Irfan say the unit-test week 'doesn't count'?
qa.a: Irfan seems defensive, minimising and finding a reason to set aside the growing pattern so there is no need to look at it.

qa.q: What turning point could Pooja offer at this stage?
qa.a: Pooja could calmly point out the move from Saturdays to Wednesdays to three times a week, and encourage Irfan to talk with a trusted adult or school counsellor about the stress behind it.

qa.q: What might Pooja be feeling as Irfan keeps talking?
qa.a: Pooja's face shows concern; hearing the story change from two to three times, plus 'don't tell Ammi', may leave Pooja worried and unsure about keeping the secret.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager's drinking spreading from weekends to weekdays while they insist they can stop and point to a friend who does worse.

passage:
Vikas bhaiya,
I know Mummy told you about the vape she found. Please don't freak out.
It's not a big deal. I only use it on weekends. Okay, and sometimes after tuition, when I'm stressed. But I can stop whenever I want. I've gone three whole days without it.
And honestly, compared to my friends, I'm nothing. Ritika uses hers all day. Sameer's in the washroom every break. I'm the careful one.
I just don't get why everyone's acting like I'm some kind of addict. It helps me calm down. That's it.
Don't tell Papa.
Dolma

qa.q: When does Dolma say she uses the vape?
qa.a: On weekends, and sometimes after tuition when stressed.

qa.q: What is Dolma feeling as she writes this letter?
qa.a: Dolma feels defensive and anxious, minimising her use and comparing herself to friends to avoid looking at the pattern.

qa.q: What could Vikas do that would help at this stage?
qa.a: Stay calm, ask what the vape helps with, and help Dolma talk to a parent or counsellor about the stress rather than lecturing.

qa.q: How might Vikas see Dolma's comparisons?
qa.a: Vikas may notice that "compared to my friends" and "I can stop" are ways of avoiding the real pattern, and feel worried.

grounding: Shows a teen minimising and comparing growing vaping use, insisting it can be stopped at any time.

passage:
Saurabh, you worry too much. Yes, I'm playing more. So what? Every day after school, and on weekends, yeah, most of the night. But I can stop whenever. I just don't want to.
And look at Kartik. He hasn't slept properly in a month. He fails every test. I'm nothing like that. I still passed my maths, sort of.
My mum took my charger last week. I used my cousin's. Doesn't matter.
Why does everyone make it such a big deal? It's just a game. It's how I relax. I'm Pradeep, and I'm fine. Seriously. Stop looking at me like that.

qa.q: What did Pradeep's mum take last week?
qa.a: Pradeep's charger.

qa.q: What is Pradeep feeling as he compares himself to Kartik?
qa.a: Pradeep feels defensive and irritated, minimising his gaming by pointing to someone who seems worse.

qa.q: What could Saurabh do next to help?
qa.a: Stay calm, say he's worried because he cares, and encourage Pradeep to talk to a parent or a counsellor.

qa.q: What is Saurabh experiencing as Pradeep talks?
qa.a: Saurabh seems worried and uncomfortable, noticing the gaming is spreading into nights and tests.

grounding: Shows a teen defending growing gaming, claiming to be able to stop whenever and pointing to a friend who is worse.

passage:
September: Ira tried a vape at a sleepover. "Just once," she told Arohi on the way home.
October: Ira bought her own. "Only on Fridays," she said. When Arohi raised an eyebrow, Ira laughed. "Relax. Meenal does it every day. I'm nowhere near that."
November: Ira was using it before school and after tuition. Arohi found her in the bathroom at a friend's house. "Ira, it's every day now."
"I can stop anytime," Ira snapped. "I just don't want to." Arohi walked away, worried. That evening she went to the school counsellor and asked what she could do to help a friend.

qa.q: When did Ira first try a vape?
qa.a: In September, at a sleepover.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling when she snapped at Arohi in November?
qa.a: Ira felt defensive and cornered, insisting she could stop so she wouldn't have to face the pattern.

qa.q: What did Arohi do that helped, and why?
qa.a: She went to the school counsellor that evening for advice, bringing in a trusted adult instead of carrying it alone.

qa.q: What is Arohi experiencing across the three months?
qa.a: Arohi grows more worried and uneasy as Ira's use increases and her excuses change.

grounding: Shows a teen's vaping growing from once to daily while she minimises and compares, and a worried friend turning to a counsellor.

passage: "Jasleen, you asked why I get so serious when your friends joke about vaping. When I was sixteen, it was cigarettes behind the bus depot. First only on Saturdays with the boys. Then Saturdays and Wednesdays. Then most days. If anyone asked, I had my answers ready. 'I can stop whenever I want.' 'Look at Bittu, he smokes twice as much as me.' I said it so often I believed it. Once I tried to stop for a week, just to prove it, and lasted two days. I told myself two days proved I could. That is how clever the mind gets when it doesn't want to look. It was my Nani who finally asked me, calmly, 'What does it do for you, beta?' I had no quick answer. That question sent me to the school counsellor. So yes, your Abhinav mama knows those lines by heart."

qa.q: Where did young Abhinav smoke?
qa.a: Behind the bus depot.

qa.q: Why did young Abhinav keep comparing himself with Bittu?
qa.a: He was uneasy about his own pattern, and the comparison let him feel safe instead of looking at it.

qa.q: What turning point came inside the story?
qa.a: Nani calmly asked what smoking did for him, which left him without a quick answer and sent him to the school counsellor.

qa.q: How might Nani have felt when asking that question?
qa.a: Nani was probably worried but chose calm curiosity over anger, hoping he would answer honestly.

grounding: Shows a teen whose use grows from weekly to most days while he insists he can stop anytime and compares himself with friends who do worse.
